Neonatal individuals of the Southern grasshopper mouse emerge weighing just 2.6 grams [Wwb = 2.6 grams], a remarkably modest birth mass that underscores the altricial state of the newborn pups. This initial size necessitates an intensive period of maternal investment, as the altricial neonates are entirely dependent on thermoregulatory and nutritional support from the female. The gestation period that precedes this live birth is surprisingly compact given the predatory lifestyle of this species; at a body temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the time from zygote formation to parturition is approximately 30 days [tg = approximately 30 days]. This relatively brief uterine phase is characteristic of many small-bodied cricetid rodents that balance rapid offspring production with the energetic demands of a carnivorous diet. Following parturition, the newborn pups attach quickly to the teats and enter an intensive phase of nursing. The onset of lactation occurs almost immediately after birth, and the milk-dependent young grow rapidly within the sheltered nest environment. The entire suite of early developmental events unfolds under the controlled thermal conditions of the maternal burrow, which helps maintain the 36 °C core temperature necessary for efficient metabolic processing during embryogenesis and early postnatal life.

The progression from a nursing pup to a nutritionally independent juvenile is marked by the completion of weaning, which occurs at 20 days after birth [tx = 20 days after birth] under the standard thermal regime of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. At this developmental milestone, the young attain a wet weight at weaning of approximately 9.2 grams [Wwx = approximately 9.2 grams], reflecting the substantial mass gain achieved during the suckling period. This dietary transition from milk to solid, insect-rich food represents a critical nutritional emancipation, coinciding with the young animal's ability to begin processing the arthropod prey that forms the bulk of the species' diet. The pre-weaning juvenile phase is therefore a period of extraordinary growth efficiency, during which body mass more than triples from the 2.6 gram neonatal value. Following weaning, the young enter a juvenile stage characterized by independent foraging and continued somatic expansion. The ultimate wet weight, representing the asymptotic adult body mass attained by fully grown individuals, reaches 22 grams [Wwi = 22 grams]. This adult mass is modest compared to many other murid rodents, reflecting the energetic constraints imposed by a diet of scorpions, grasshoppers, and other invertebrates.

Females of this species reach reproductive maturity, or puberty, at 41 days after birth [tp = 41 days after birth] when maintained at a body temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This rapid progression from birth to sexual maturity is consistent with a life-history strategy geared toward high population turnover in unpredictable desert environments. The onset of gonadal activity marks the transition from the juvenile stage to the breeding adult mammal phase, during which females become capable of sustaining the energetic demands of gestation and lactation. Once reproductively active, the maximum reproductive output is expressed through a combination of litter size and breeding frequency. Available data indicate that females most commonly produce litters of approximately 3.7 pups [N_R_i = approximately 3.7 pups] per reproductive event, and field observations suggest they can achieve approximately 2.7 litters annually [F_R_i = approximately 2.7 litters annually]. This reproductive schedule allows for sustained recruitment even when juvenile mortality is high, a common challenge for small-bodied predators inhabiting arid ecosystems.

Longevity data for Onychomys torridus remain somewhat uncertain, but the best available estimates suggest a maximum lifespan of approximately 4.6 years [am = approximately 4.6 years] when individuals are maintained at a stable body temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This lifespan, though modest by mammalian standards, is comparatively long for a rodent of its small body mass and likely reflects the benefits of a protein-rich diet and reduced predation pressure in its semi-fossorial lifestyle. Natural mortality in the wild often results from avian and reptilian predators, though senescence-related physiological deterioration contributes to age-related death in captive settings. The species' relatively slow aging rate, given its high reproductive output, remains a topic of interest among life-history ecologists studying trade-offs between fecundity and somatic maintenance in desert-adapted rodents. Confirming the exact limits of this species' longevity will require additional mark-recapture studies and longitudinal captive observations.

The life history of Onychomys torridus is shaped by the arid ecosystems it inhabits, where food availability fluctuates dramatically with seasonal rainfall. For a breeding adult mammal investing heavily in each litter, the ability to sustain a core body temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] during cold desert nights is critical for both maternal survival and offspring development. The entire schedule from parturition to weaning is remarkably compressed; the time since birth at weaning of 20 days within a 30 day gestation interval allows females to produce multiple cohorts within a single favorable season. This rapid pace of development, combined with the onset of puberty at 41 days after birth [tp = 41 days after birth], enables populations to rebound quickly following periods of low resource availability at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C].
